title: Revenue rolled up to top-level categories (recursive CTE)
problem_md:
Products are attached to categories at any depth of a category tree stored as an adjacency list
(`parent_id` is `NULL` for top-level categories). Some products are attached directly to a top-level category.
The CEO wants revenue **rolled up to each top-level category**, including every descendant category at any depth.

```sql
CREATE TABLE categories (
  category_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  parent_id   INTEGER REFERENCES categories(category_id)   -- NULL = top level
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  product_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         TEXT NOT NULL,
  category_id INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  product_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
  quantity      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  unit_price    REAL NOT NULL
);
```

> Money columns are `REAL` in this sandbox (they would be `NUMERIC(12,2)` in production PostgreSQL). Dates are ISO `'YYYY-MM-DD'` text.

**Task.** Return `top_category` (name of the top-level category) and `revenue` (sum of `quantity * unit_price` of
all order items whose product sits in that category or any descendant). Top-level categories with no sales must
appear with `0`. Order by `revenue` descending, then `top_category`.

examples.input: Festive Kurtas (9) -> Kurtas (6) -> Women (3) -> Fashion (1); TOTE-BAG is attached directly to Fashion; Grocery has a product but no sales

hints: First map every category to its top-level ancestor. Because depth is unbounded, you need `WITH RECURSIVE`.

Anchor: `SELECT category_id, name AS top_category FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL`. Recursive step: join `categories c` where `c.parent_id` equals a row already in the CTE, carrying `top_category` down.
Then `tree LEFT JOIN products LEFT JOIN order_items`, `GROUP BY top_category`, `COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0)`.
starter_code:
-- Write your query here
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  -- anchor: top-level categories
  SELECT ...
  UNION ALL
  -- recursive step: children of rows already in tree
  SELECT ...
)
SELECT ...
solution_code:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT category_id, name AS top_category
  FROM categories
  WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.category_id, t.top_category
  FROM categories c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.category_id
)
SELECT t.top_category,
       COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 0) AS revenue
FROM tree t
LEFT JOIN products p     ON p.category_id = t.category_id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY t.top_category
ORDER BY revenue DESC, t.top_category;
solution_md:
**Recursive CTE anatomy.**

1. **Anchor member** - the top-level categories, each labelled with its own name as `top_category`.
2. **Recursive member** - children of any row already produced (`c.parent_id = t.category_id`), inheriting the
   ancestor's label. It runs repeatedly on the rows produced by the previous iteration until no new rows appear.
3. `UNION ALL` glues iterations together (use `UNION` only if you need duplicate elimination, e.g. to stop cycles).

The CTE yields one row per category: `(4, Fashion)`, `(9, Fashion)` (three levels down), `(8, Beauty)`, and the
roots themselves - which is why the tote bag attached directly to *Fashion* is counted.

**Aggregation.** `LEFT JOIN` all the way down keeps categories without products/sales; their `SUM` is NULL and
`COALESCE` turns it into 0 (Grocery). An inner join would silently drop Grocery.

Fashion = 998 + 1999 + 1299 + 2499 + 899 = 7694; Beauty = 1047 + 1300 = 2347.

**Safety.** Bad data (a category that is its own ancestor) makes a recursive CTE loop forever. Guard with a depth
column (`t.depth + 1 ... WHERE t.depth < 20`) or, in PostgreSQL 14+, the `CYCLE` clause:
`... ) CYCLE category_id SET is_cycle USING path`.

**The same in PostgreSQL** - identical syntax (`WITH RECURSIVE` is required there too). For deep or frequently
queried trees, consider storing a materialized path (`ltree` extension, e.g. `fashion.women.kurtas`) or a closure
table so roll-ups become a single indexed join. Index `categories (parent_id)` so each recursive step is an index
lookup, plus `products (category_id)` and `order_items (product_id)` for the joins.
